lessons.title: Types of Rabbit Housing: Hutches, Cages, and Colonies
lessons.body: When starting with rabbits in Africa, you have three main housing choices: hutches, cages, and colony systems. Each has pros and cons depending on your climate, budget, and space. Hutches are usually small wooden or wire structures raised off the ground. They work well for a few rabbits. A typical hutch is 90 cm long, 60 cm wide, and 45 cm high, costing about $20-30 to build from local timber and wire mesh. Cages are made entirely of wire mesh, often galvanised, and are stacked or hung under a roof. They are easy to clean and protect against predators. A good cage for a breeding doe is 80 cm x 60 cm x 40 cm. Colonies let rabbits live together in a large pen or floor area, like a small room or fenced yard with a wire floor. This mimics nature but can lead to fighting and disease spread. In Africa, the best choice for most smallholders is a combination: wire cages for breeding and growing, and a colony pen for exercise or for meat production if managed well. Consider your climate: in hot areas, wire cages with good airflow are best; in cooler highlands, wooden hutches with insulation may be needed. Always raise housing at least 1 metre off the ground to prevent dampness and predator attacks. Use local materials like bamboo, eucalyptus poles, and offcuts from timber yards to cut costs. Remember, rabbits need protection from direct sun, rain, and strong winds. A simple roof of corrugated iron sheets or thatch will do. Whatever you choose, ensure each adult rabbit has at least 0.5 square metres of floor space, and kits (young rabbits) have 0.2 square metres. Overcrowding causes stress, disease, and fighting. Start small with two or three cages, then expand as your herd grows.

lessons.title: Designing a Rabbitry Layout
lessons.body: A rabbitry is the building or area where you keep your rabbits. A good layout saves you time, reduces disease, and makes daily work easier. Start by choosing a site that is slightly sloping so water drains away, and at least 30 metres from other livestock to avoid disease spread. The rabbitry should face east-west to minimise direct sunlight on the cages. Plan for three main zones: breeding area, growing area, and quarantine area. The breeding area holds your does (females) and bucks (males). Keep bucks separate from does except for mating. Each breeding cage should be 80 cm x 60 cm x 40 cm. The growing area is for weaned kits (young rabbits) from 4 weeks to slaughter at 12-16 weeks. These can be in group cages of 1.5 m x 1 m x 40 cm, holding up to 10 rabbits. The quarantine area is for new or sick rabbits, placed at least 5 metres away and downwind. A simple layout: a central walkway 1 metre wide, with cages on both sides, stacked two or three tiers high. Leave 30 cm between tiers for ventilation and cleaning. The roof should extend 50 cm beyond the cages to keep rain out. Use wire mesh floors (1.5 cm x 1.5 cm holes) so droppings fall through. Under the cages, put a concrete floor sloping to a drain for easy cleaning. If you have limited space, a 3 m x 4 m shed can hold 12-16 cages. In hot climates, add a ridge vent and open sides with wire mesh; in cooler areas, use removable plastic sheeting. Always keep a footbath with disinfectant at the entrance. This layout reduces stress on you and the rabbits, and helps prevent disease outbreaks.

lessons.title: Materials for Building Rabbit Hutches
lessons.body: You don't need expensive imported materials to build strong rabbit hutches. In Africa, you can use locally available items: timber, bamboo, wire mesh, corrugated iron sheets, and nails. For the frame, use hardwood like eucalyptus or mahogany poles (5-7 cm diameter) or treated pine. Avoid softwoods that rot quickly. Bamboo is cheap and strong but must be dried and treated against termites by soaking in used engine oil or borax solution. For the sides and floor, use galvanised wire mesh with 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm holes for adults and 1 cm x 1 cm for kits. This allows droppings to fall through and prevents predators. A 1 m x 2 m roll of wire mesh costs about $10-15. For the roof, use corrugated iron sheets (gauge 30) or thatch. Iron sheets last longer but get hot; paint them white or use a double layer with an air gap to reduce heat. Thatch is cooler but needs replacing every 2-3 years. For the nest box, use plywood or old wooden boxes, 40 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm, with a 15 cm high lip to keep kits in. Avoid using chicken wire for floors as it causes foot sores. Use 16-gauge wire for structural parts. Nails and screws should be galvanised to prevent rust. For door latches, use simple hooks and eyes or wooden pegs. A basic 3-cage unit (each 80x60x40 cm) costs around $50-70 in materials. Always sand rough edges and ensure no sharp wire ends protrude. Treat all wood with a rabbit-safe preservative like lime wash or borax. Never use creosote or old engine oil directly on surfaces rabbits can chew. With careful work, a hutch can last 5-7 years.

lessons.title: Essential Equipment: Feeders, Waterers, Nest Boxes
lessons.body: Rabbits need constant access to clean feed and water. For feeders, use ceramic or metal hoppers that attach to the cage wire. A good hopper holds 1-2 kg of pellets and costs $5-10. You can make your own from a plastic jerrycan cut open and wired to the cage, but ensure no sharp edges. For hay, use a wire rack outside the cage so rabbits pull strands through. Avoid open bowlsârabbits will soil them. For waterers, use nipple drinkers connected to a plastic bottle or a small bucket with a lid. Nipple drinkers cost $2-3 each and prevent spillage and contamination. In hot climates, check water twice daily; a lactating doe drinks up to 2 litres a day. If you use bottles, clean them every 3 days with a bottle brush and mild bleach solution. Nest boxes are for kindling (giving birth). Provide a wooden box 40 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm with a 15 cm high front lip. Line it with soft dry grass, wood shavings, or shredded paper. Put the nest box in the doe's cage 3 days before kindling (day 28 of pregnancy). After kindling, check for dead kits and remove them. Clean and disinfect the nest box between litters. For feed storage, use metal or plastic bins with tight lids to keep out rats and moisture. A 50 kg feed bag should be stored off the floor on a pallet. Also get a small scale (up to 5 kg) to weigh rabbits and feed. A record book and pen are essential to track breeding dates, kindling, and weights. Total equipment cost for 10 cages: about $80-120. Buy from local agrovet shops or online. Always have spare drinkers and feedersâthey break.

lessons.title: Climate Control and Ventilation
lessons.body: Rabbits are sensitive to heat and drafts. In Africa, heat stress is a major killer. Ideal temperature is 18-24Â°C. Above 30Â°C, rabbits stop eating, pant, and can die. Below 10Â°C, especially for kits, they need protection. To cool your rabbitry: build in shade, use reflective roofs (white paint or aluminium), and open sides with wire mesh for airflow. A ridge vent at the roof peak lets hot air escape. In very hot areas, use a fan or wet gunny sacks on the windward side to cool incoming air. Misting the roof with water in the afternoon helps. For cold: in highlands, use removable plastic curtains on the sides, and provide nest boxes with extra bedding. Never seal the rabbitry completelyâammonia from urine builds up and causes respiratory disease. Aim for 10-15 air changes per hour. You can test ventilation by holding a candle flame near the cage; if it flickers, air is moving. But avoid direct drafts on rabbits. In humid coastal areas, use dehumidifiers or charcoal in trays to absorb moisture. Always provide shadeâa simple thatch roof or shade cloth (70% shade) works. Plant trees like mango or neem around the rabbitry for natural cooling. In dry dusty areas, sprinkle water on the floor to settle dust. Monitor temperature with a cheap thermometer ($2-3). If rabbits lie stretched out and pant, it's too hot. If they huddle, it's too cold. Adjust curtains, fans, or water mist accordingly. Remember, sudden temperature changes cause stress. Keep conditions stable.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Sanitation Tools
lessons.body: Dirty cages cause disease. You need a simple cleaning kit: a stiff-bristled hand brush, a scraper (like a putty knife), a bucket, a watering can, and disinfectant. For daily cleaning, remove soiled bedding and droppings from under cages with a rake or shovel. Use a wheelbarrow to carry waste to a compost pit. Once a week, scrub feeders and waterers with a brush and hot soapy water, then rinse and dry in the sun. Once a month, do a deep clean: remove rabbits to a temporary cage, scrape all surfaces, wash with a disinfectant solution (1 part bleach to 10 parts water, or 2% formalin), and let dry. Never mix bleach and ammoniaâit creates toxic gas. For wire cages, use a wire brush to remove hair and scale. For wooden hutches, scrub with a mild bleach solution and let sun-dry. Use a flame torch (carefully) to singe off hair and parasites on metal cages. For floors, sweep and mop with disinfectant. Keep a footbath with disinfectant at the entranceâuse a shallow tray with a sponge or sawdust soaked in 2% caustic soda. Change footbath daily. Wear gloves and boots when cleaning. After handling sick rabbits, wash hands and change clothes. Store cleaning tools separate from feed. Have a dedicated bin for waste. Compost manure for 3-6 months before using on crops. A good sanitation routine takes 15 minutes daily and 1 hour weekly. It prevents coccidiosis, ear mites, and respiratory infections. Always keep the rabbitry dryâmoisture breeds bacteria. Use a squeegee to remove standing water. With consistent cleaning, your rabbits will be healthy and productive.

quiz.q: What is the minimum floor space recommended for an adult rabbit?
quiz.explanation: Each adult rabbit needs at least 0.5 square metres to reduce stress and fighting.

quiz.q: Which housing type is best for a smallholder in a hot climate?
options: A) Wooden hutch with solid walls
B) Wire cage with good airflow
C) Colony pen on the ground
quiz.explanation: Wire cages allow maximum ventilation, which is critical in hot climates to prevent heat stress.

quiz.q: How high should rabbit housing be raised off the ground?
quiz.explanation: Raising housing at least 1 metre off the ground prevents dampness and predator attacks.

quiz.q: What is the ideal size for a breeding doe's cage?
options: A) 40 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm
B) 60 cm x 40 cm x 30 cm
C) 80 cm x 60 cm x 40 cm
D) 100 cm x 80 cm x 50 cm
quiz.explanation: A cage of 80 cm x 60 cm x 40 cm provides enough space for a doe and her litter.

quiz.q: In a rabbitry layout, where should the quarantine area be placed?
options: A) Next to the breeding area
B) At least 5 metres away and downwind
C) In the centre of the rabbitry
quiz.explanation: Quarantine must be isolated and downwind to prevent disease spread to healthy rabbits.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a ridge vent in a rabbitry roof?
options: B) To allow hot air to escape
quiz.explanation: A ridge vent at the roof peak allows hot air to escape, improving ventilation.

quiz.q: Which material is best for the floor of a rabbit cage?
options: B) Galvanised wire mesh with 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm holes
quiz.explanation: Wire mesh with 1.5 cm holes allows droppings to fall through and prevents foot sores.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using chicken wire for rabbit cage floors?
quiz.explanation: Chicken wire has thin, sharp wires that can injure rabbits' feet, leading to sores.

quiz.q: What is a safe preservative for treating wood used in rabbit hutches?
quiz.explanation: Lime wash is rabbit-safe; creosote and engine oil are toxic if chewed.

quiz.q: How much does a basic 3-cage unit cost in materials approximately?
quiz.explanation: Using local materials, a 3-cage unit costs about $50-70.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for a nest box?
options: A) 20 cm x 20 cm x 20 cm
B) 40 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm
C) 60 cm x 40 cm x 40 cm
D) 80 cm x 60 cm x 40 cm
quiz.explanation: A nest box of 40 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm with a 15 cm lip is ideal for kindling.

quiz.q: When should a nest box be placed in a doe's cage?
quiz.explanation: Placing the nest box 3 days before kindling (day 28 of pregnancy) gives the doe time to prepare.

quiz.q: What type of waterer is best to prevent spillage and contamination?
quiz.explanation: Nipple drinkers provide clean water and prevent spillage and contamination.

quiz.q: How often should water bottles be cleaned?
quiz.explanation: Clean water bottles every 3 days with a brush and mild bleach solution.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Rabbits are most comfortable and productive between 18-24Â°C.

quiz.q: What sign indicates heat stress in rabbits?
options: B) Lying stretched out and panting
quiz.explanation: When hot, rabbits stretch out and pant to lose heat.

quiz.q: How can you improve ventilation in a rabbitry?
options: B) Use open sides with wire mesh and a ridge vent
quiz.explanation: Open sides with wire mesh and a ridge vent allow good airflow.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for adequate ventilation?
options: A) Hold a candle flame near the cage; it should flicker
quiz.explanation: A flickering candle flame indicates air movement, but avoid direct drafts on rabbits.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to mix bleach and ammonia when cleaning?
options: A) It creates a bad smell
quiz.explanation: Mixing bleach and ammonia releases toxic chloramine gas, which is harmful to breathe.

quiz.q: How often should you do a deep clean of the rabbitry?
quiz.explanation: A monthly deep clean with disinfectant helps prevent disease build-up.

quiz.q: What is the correct dilution for bleach disinfectant?
options: A) 1 part bleach to 1 part water
B) 1 part bleach to 10 parts water
C) 1 part bleach to 100 parts water
quiz.explanation: A 1:10 bleach-to-water solution is effective and safe for most surfaces.

quiz.q: What should you use to singe off hair and parasites from metal cages?
quiz.explanation: A flame torch can be used carefully to burn off hair and parasites on metal cages.

quiz.q: How long should manure be composted before use on crops?
quiz.explanation: Composting for 3-6 months kills pathogens and parasites before using manure on crops.

quiz.q: What is a footbath used for?
quiz.explanation: A footbath with disinfectant helps prevent carrying disease into the rabbitry.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for daily cleaning under cages?
quiz.explanation: A rake or shovel is used to remove droppings and soiled bedding from under cages.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store feed to prevent pests?
options: A) In an open bag on the floor
B) In a metal or plastic bin with tight lid
quiz.explanation: Metal or plastic bins with tight lids keep out rats and moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you keep cleaning tools separate from feed?
quiz.explanation: Separating tools prevents cross-contamination of feed with harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade cloth percentage for rabbitries?
quiz.explanation: 70% shade cloth provides adequate cooling without blocking too much light.

quiz.q: How often should you check water supply in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: In hot weather, rabbits drink more, so check water twice daily.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a quarantine area?
options: A) To isolate new or sick rabbits
quiz.explanation: Quarantine prevents disease spread by isolating new or sick rabbits.
